title: A penalty-interior-point algorithm for nonlinear constrained optimization
contribution: PIPAL: a penalty-interior-point method whose closed-form slack reset removes a merit parameter and whose penalty and barrier parameters are chosen inside each iteration from a few candidate values by model-reduction tests, with one factorization per iteration; competitive with IPOPT on CUTEr and more robust on constructed degenerate and infeasible variants (pp. 1, 8-19, 22-28).
problem_entry: Penalty methods regularize and detect infeasibility but need LP/QP subproblems; IPMs scale but lack constraint regularization and converge slowly to infeasible stationary points; combine them and make the parameter updates the contribution (pp. 1-3).
key_idea: Subproblem (1.5) with slack reset (3.4) so (1.5)'s constraints always hold; in each iteration pick the largest admissible rho from candidates by (3.16)-(3.18), then the largest mu nearly minimizing quality function (3.20)-(3.21); fall back to the conservative PIPAL-c direction if no pair is admissible (pp. 3, 8-19).
assumptions: f, c C1 (Assumption 2.1, p. 5); reduced-Hessian positivity (Assumption 3.1, p. 9) enforced by identity shifts (p. 19); equalities via c + a - b = 0 to keep MFCQ of the penalty subproblem (p. 20); no convergence theorem for the adaptive algorithm, only 'motivated' (pp. 1, 5, 15).
proof_devices: regularity facts stated without proof: MFCQ of penalty and penalty-IPM subproblems, mu -> 0 limits, exact-penalty threshold (Theorems 2.2-2.8, pp. 5-7)
directional-derivative identity (3.6) under the closed-form slack reset (Theorem 3.2, pp. 9-10)
linearity of the Newton right-hand side in (rho, mu): any pair's direction from three solves with one factorization ((4.3), p. 18)
experiments: Matlab; PIPAL-c, PIPAL-a, IPOPT 3.9 (MA27) on AMPL CUTEr, presolve off; 438 -> 417 models after stated filters; iteration counts in pairwise bar profiles and Dolan-More profile; IPOPT more efficient on the full set, PIPAL-a better on the 132 problems where PIPAL-c reduced rho; degenerate (120) and infeasible (105) HS variants favour PIPAL; IPOPT engineering adopted; parameters tuned on the runs; one ablation without numbers (pp. 17-27).
positioning: Lists penalty-barrier and penalty-IPM relatives as differing in detail and classifies their parameter updates as conservative; claims first combination of steering [9] and adaptive barrier [28] rules; concedes IPOPT's efficiency (pp. 4, 11-13, 28).
writing: Hedged contribution sentences ('we believe', 'novel and sound'); design choices justified by the failure of the alternative tried; each constructed test set introduced with 'the picture is much different'; conclusion = two strengths plus one concession plus application contexts (pp. 4, 16, 25-28).
limits_future: Stated: extra degrees of freedom may slow convergence, needs a more sophisticated implementation, rho may be reduced too far, one type of degeneracy (pp. 24-25, 28); visible: no convergence theorem, iteration counts only, tuned parameters, unquantified ablation (pp. 5, 15, 21, 27); future: general-purpose solver, MPCC, MINLP (p. 28).

method_links.note: Contribution is the in-iteration update of penalty and barrier parameters from model-predicted feasibility progress; final rho values tabulated.
Step 4 (prove fast local convergence to infeasible stationary points) not done: the rate is imported from [5] as a hope via condition (3.18).
Degenerate (-c_i^2 <= 0) and infeasible (c_i^2 <= -1) HS variants, presolve off, narrowness of the construction admitted.

IPOPT's bound relaxation, initial point, scaling, minimum values and evaluation-error handling adopted 'for a fairer comparison'; in-framework conservative rival PIPAL-c; IPOPT's efficiency win printed.
Parameters set to the values giving the best results in the experiments; an ablation reported without numbers (and apparently citing the wrong condition number).

new_pattern_candidates.evidence: Because (rho, mu) enter only the right-hand side, directions for all 25 candidate pairs are linear combinations of three solves with one factorization.
After the full-set profile, the comparison is repeated on the 132 problems where the conservative baseline had to decrease rho, which is where the adaptive rule should matter.
If no (rho, mu) pair is admissible, PIPAL-a uses the conservative PIPAL-c direction.

transferable: Eliminate slack variables in closed form at every iterate so the constraints always hold and the merit function needs no balancing parameter ((3.3)-(3.4), pp. 8-9).
Freeze the KKT matrix within an iteration and get the step for any (rho, mu) by linear combination of three solves ((4.3), p. 18).
Choose the largest mu whose quality value is within a factor of the best rather than the minimizer, to avoid driving mu to zero for marginal gains ((3.21), p. 16).
Import the incumbent's preprocessing and safeguards into the prototype before comparing, listing each with its source (pp. 20-21).
Build the comparison in three layers: full set, subset where the mechanism fired, constructed degenerate and infeasible sets (pp. 22-27).
coauthors: none (sole author; R. A. Waltz helped with software, p. 28)

quotes.text: After all, in the context of Algorithm 1, each distinct value for the penalty parameter ρ potentially requires the computational efforts of a complete run of a standard interior-point algorithm.
Our experiments support the claim that when an interior-point method is performing at its best, it is difficult to outperform such an approach in terms of efficiency.

title: A note on the implementation of an interior-point algorithm for nonlinear optimization with inexact step computations
contribution: Implements the inexact interior-point algorithm of Curtis-Schenk-Waechter (2010) in Ipopt with PARDISO's iterative solver, using the cheap single-system SMART-test step by default and the rank-robust decomposition step only after short steps, reaching 89% robustness on CUTE and speedups up to 17.89 on 3-D PDE-constrained problems (pp. 2-18).
problem_entry: Interior-point methods become impractical at large scale because factorizations fill in; PDE-constrained optimization is the target; the paper is an implementation note for the algorithm of [13] (pp. 2-3).
key_idea: Iterative solves of the primal-dual system stopped by SMART tests on the merit-model reduction; switch from the one-system Algorithm 2 to the normal/tangential Algorithm 3 when the accepted steplength drops below 1e-3, since Algorithm 2's proof needs steplengths bounded away from zero; Hessian modification triggered by the tests; flexible penalty; adaptive preconditioner refinement (pp. 5-11).
assumptions: Smooth (e.g. C2) problem functions (p. 2); global convergence inherited from [13] for Algorithm 1 + 3 (p. 9); practical primal-dual barrier Hessian kept between multiples of the analysed primal one so the analysis applies (pp. 10-11).
proof_devices: no new theorems; merit-model reduction as a bound on the directional derivative (p. 6)
Cauchy decrease for the inexact trust-region normal step (p. 9)
sandwich of the practical primal-dual Sigma between nu*mu*S^-2 multiples to inherit the primal analysis (pp. 10-11)
experiments: Ipopt rev. 1954 + PARDISO 4.1.1 SQMR with multilevel preconditioner; 617 CUTE problems: 89% vs 96% default Ipopt vs 84% always-Algorithm-3, 142 switches (p. 12); boundary control (up to 670k variables) speedups 4.34-7.85 and server-room cooling (up to 664k variables) speedups 2.64-17.89 at equal iteration counts and objective values; late-iteration preconditioner degradation reported (pp. 12-17).
positioning: Full-space PDE-optimization method with strong guarantees and computational flexibility, contrasted with nonlinear elimination and reduced-space approaches; convex-case relative-residual termination [14] insufficient for nonconvex problems (pp. 2, 6).
writing: Short note that names what is omitted and where it lives (full report [10]); all parameter values listed; claims tied to tables; conclusion restates design and one open problem (pp. 3, 7, 9-11, 14, 18).
limits_future: Preconditioner effectiveness falls as mu -> 0, handling log-barrier ill-conditioning in the incomplete factorization left open (p. 18); robustness below default Ipopt (p. 12); general-purpose preconditioner only, two PDE examples, no other inexact solver compared (pp. 3, 12-17).

method_links.note: SMART tests derived from the merit model stop the iterative solver; Hessian modification triggered by the tests' curvature condition, not inertia; timed in a production code at scale.
Flexible penalty interval steers the merit parameter, but the step computation switches between two algorithms on a steplength trigger (within one outer algorithm).
Always-guaranteed variant of [13] run as an in-framework rival (84% vs 89%); default Ipopt's higher robustness printed; worst preconditioner behaviour described.

new_pattern_candidates.evidence: Use the single-system inexact step and switch to the regularized decomposition step only when the accepted steplength falls below 1e-3, the quantity Algorithm 2's convergence proof needs bounded away from zero.
The always-regularized, fully guaranteed variant of [13] solves 84% of CUTE vs 89% for the switching implementation, measuring what the guarantee costs.

transferable: Monitor the quantity the cheap method's convergence proof needs (here the steplength) and switch to the guaranteed method only when it collapses (pp. 9-10).
Sandwich a practical component between multiples of the analysed one and enforce the bounds, so the existing proof still applies (pp. 10-11).
Escalate inside the inner solver before changing the outer algorithm: tighten drop tolerances, retry, then switch step algorithm (p. 10).
Report per-mesh-level tables with iterations, objective, total and per-iteration CPU time and speedup (Tables 2 and 4, pp. 13, 17).
Scale discretized PDE constraints by powers of h so their gradients do not vanish under refinement (pp. 13, 16).
coauthors: Johannes Huber, Olaf Schenk, Andreas Waechter

quotes.text: Specifically, the computation time for the largest instance with more than 600,000 variables was reduced from more than 6 days to 8.2 h, a speedup by a factor of 17.89.
As mentioned at the end of Sect. 4.1, we have observed a decrease in effectiveness of the preconditioner as the barrier parameter approaches zero.

title: An adaptive gradient sampling algorithm for nonsmooth optimization
contribution: Adaptive gradient sampling (AGS): reuses sampled gradients so only O(1) new gradients are needed per iteration, warm-starts the QO solver, adds two bounded variable-metric updates built from sample-point information, and keeps GS's probability-one convergence; more progress than GS within a fixed gradient budget (pp. 2-21).
problem_entry: Three numbered practical limitations of gradient sampling: n+1 fresh gradients per iteration, QO subproblems solved from scratch, steepest-descent-like behaviour (p. 3).
key_idea: Keep gradients still in the epsilon-ball, add p-bar new samples, allow incomplete line searches that trigger more sampling, seed the QO active set from the previous iteration, and use L-BFGS on sampled directions or a rank-one overestimation update with bounded conditioning; GS is the special case p-bar = p, H = I (pp. 3-12).
assumptions: f locally Lipschitz and C1 on an open dense set (Assumption 4.1, p. 12); uniformly bounded positive definite H_k (Assumption 3.1, p. 6), proved for both updates; bounds worst-case and not tight in practice, so guarantee-free variants are also tested (pp. 6, 9, 11-12).
proof_devices: per-update bound lemma for BFGS with skip rules, iterated over at most p+1 updates, Rayleigh-Ritz for the inverse (Lemma 3.2, Theorem 3.3, pp. 7-9)
rank-one overestimation stretch with rho in [0, sqrt(2 rho)-1] giving (2 rho)^(p+1) conditioning; inert for convex f (Theorems 3.6, 3.8, pp. 10-12)
QO KKT conditions give grad f(x_k)^T d_k <= -d_k^T H_k d_k (Lemma 4.3, p. 13)
incomplete line searches cannot repeat forever because the sample count grows (Lemma 4.4, p. 13)
Caratheodory-based open set of good sample sets; staying outside it is a probability-zero event (Lemma 4.7 and Cases 1a-1b, pp. 15-17), following Kiwiel
experiments: Matlab with a specialized active-set QO solver; 26 scalable nonsmooth problems, n = 50, 10 runs each (fixed and 9 random starts); six variants in one code (Table 1); measures: final sampling radius at a 100n gradient budget and QO iterations per nonlinear iteration; AGS beats GS, Hessian updates help, ill-conditioned guarantee-free variants do not; parameters tuned to best results; no external comparator (pp. 17-21).
positioning: Builds on Burke-Lewis-Overton and Kiwiel with point-by-point differences and explicit credit; bundle methods named as the target to match; Wolfe's conjugate subgradient discussed as a forerunner (pp. 2-3, 21).
writing: Numbered limitation list mapped to design elements; efficiency claim tied to a stated measure; unexpected and negative results flagged with possible explanations; repeated proofs justified (pp. 2-3, 13, 15, 20-21).
limits_future: n = 50 only, parameters tuned on the test set, no external comparator, heuristic mu_k update called critical (pp. 6, 18-19); future: merging gradient sampling with bundle methods and borrowing Wolfe's previous search directions (pp. 21-22).

method_links.note: Incumbent GS is a parameter setting of the same code; one-component ablation ladder of six variants; 10 runs per problem.
Parameters chosen for the best overall results on the evaluation set; no external state-of-the-art comparator.
Success not judged by a termination flag: progress is measured by the sampling radius reached within a fixed gradient-evaluation budget.

Adaptive sampling chosen partly so the inner QO solver can be warm-started, with a tailored QO solver for near-collinear gradients; but the inner tolerance is fixed (1e-10), not derived from the globalization.

new_pattern_candidates.evidence: Variants that drop the Hessian bounds required by the convergence analysis (AGS-LBFGS-ill, AGS-over-ill) are run beside the guaranteed ones; no gain, and LBFGS-ill is worse on final radius.
GS is AGS with p-bar = p >= n+1 and H_k = I, so the incumbent and all variants run in one code.

transferable: Make the incumbent a parameter setting of the new method so every comparison is one code with one knob turned (p. 5).
Keep a quasi-Newton matrix within convergence hypotheses by per-iteration reinitialization, capped update count and curvature skip rules ((9), pp. 7-9).
For methods with incomparable termination, compare the progress measure reached at a fixed evaluation budget and add a measure isolating the mechanism (p. 19).
Run the guarantee-free twin of a safeguarded component to test whether the safeguard costs performance (pp. 18, 20-21).
Reuse samples still in the neighbourhood and allow incomplete line searches that trigger more sampling instead of failing (Algorithm 2.1, p. 5).

quotes.text: Global convergence of the algorithm is proved assuming that the Hessian approximations are positive definite and bounded, an assumption shown to be true for the proposed Hessian approximation updating strategies.
The first measure shows the progress towards optimality that the solver makes within a fixed gradient evaluation limit

title: A sequential quadratic optimization algorithm with rapid infeasibility detection
contribution: SQuID: an SQO method with at most two QO solves per iteration (a pure feasibility QO, then a penalized optimality QO) and penalty and multiplier updates placed between them, proved globally convergent and quadratically convergent to both KKT points and infeasible stationary points without feasibility restoration (pp. 1-28).
problem_entry: Slow infeasibility detection hurts modelers and MINLP branch-and-bound; penalty-SQO puts the whole burden on the penalty parameter; the predecessor [6] has the fast infeasible rate but needs at least three QO solves per iteration near infeasible stationary points (pp. 1-3).
key_idea: Solve a feasibility QO (3.7) to measure attainable linearized feasibility progress; if it is small relative to v(x_k), cut rho to O(R_inf^2) and pull the optimality multipliers toward the feasibility ones before the optimality QO (3.9); combine the two directions with the smallest weight achieving a fraction of the feasibility progress; second rho update for model reduction; l1 line search (pp. 5-9).
assumptions: C2 functions (p. 4); positive definite QO Hessians (Assumption 4.1, p. 9); bounded Lipschitz functions and uniformly bounded H for global results (Assumption 4.7, p. 12); full-rank active Jacobian, strict complementarity, SOSC, exact Hessians and unit steps for local rates, called strong with named relaxation devices (Assumptions 4.19-4.20, pp. 20-21).
proof_devices: model reductions as surrogates for directional derivatives of v and the l1 penalty (Lemma 4.2, pp. 9-10)
boundedness of directions by comparison with the feasible zero step (Lemma 4.9, p. 13)
monotone shifted penalty rho(f - f_low) + v absorbing decreasing rho (Lemma 4.11, p. 14)
dichotomy: limit points all feasible or all infeasible; feasible ones with rho -> 0 are FJ points where MFCQ fails (Theorem 4.16, pp. 17-19)
implicit-function path x_rho with O(rho) distance to the infeasible stationary point (Lemma 4.22, pp. 22-23)
perturbed Newton error bound C||e||^2 + O(rho) + O(multiplier change); rho = O(||e||^2) gives quadratic rate (Theorem 4.25, pp. 25-27)
Newton analysis via Dennis-Schnabel Thm 5.2.1 for KKT points (Theorem 4.28, p. 28)
experiments: Prototype Matlab code with quadprog on 123 HS AMPL models and infeasible copies (add x1 <= 0 and x1 >= 1): 90.16% and 90.24% success with failures and one false infeasibility verdict reported and attributed to nonconvexity; last-ten-iteration log-residual plots as rate evidence; predecessor [6] compared on its six toy problems with matched parameters, fewer QO solves except on robot; no external solver (pp. 28-32).
positioning: Literature-review section: penalty-SQO criticised by mechanism; predecessor [6] credited and its QO count quantified; multiphase active-set SQO and trust-region predictor/accelerator methods distinguished by subproblem type and globalization; Burke's earlier methods closest (pp. 2-4).
writing: Two named novelties in the introduction; focus explicitly fenced against general assumptions; abstract calls the per-iteration design 'two-phase'; modest framing of prototype results; parallel sentences for the feasible and infeasible regimes in the conclusion (pp. 1-2, 30, 32).
limits_future: Stated: QO solver efficiency, Hessian modifications cumbersome at large scale and possibly blocking superlinear rates, strong local assumptions (pp. 20-21, 32); visible: HS-only Matlab prototype, no external solver, single easy infeasibility construction, implementation skips analysed branches (pp. 29-30); future: inexact QO solves and negative curvature (p. 32).

method_links.note: One algorithm for feasible and infeasible instances without feasibility restoration; penalty update placed between the two QO solves from predicted feasibility progress; fast local convergence to infeasible stationary points proved (step 4).
The paper calls its per-iteration design a 'two-phase strategy'; both phases run in every iteration, so it is not a switch.
Infeasible copy of the whole HS set by adding x1 <= 0 and x1 >= 1, already in 2014.
Only rival is the predecessor [6] on six toy problems with its parameters matched and its robot win printed; no external code, no profile.

new_pattern_candidates.evidence: log10 of the optimality and infeasibility residuals over the last ten iterations of every solved run; slopes below -1 and -2 read as superlinear and quadratic convergence.

new_pattern_candidates.pattern: separate multiplier estimates for optimization and feasibility
new_pattern_candidates.evidence: Two multiplier estimates are maintained because the algorithm must implicitly decide which of two problems it is solving; the optimality one is pulled toward the feasibility one near infeasible points.

transferable: Place the parameter update between two subproblem solves so the first solve's information changes the second solve's objective in the same iteration (p. 7).
Require the step to achieve a fixed fraction of the attainable feasibility progress by choosing the smallest convex-combination weight, found by bisection ((3.10)-(3.11), p. 7; p. 30).
Prove monotonicity of the shifted merit rho(f - f_low) + v to handle a decreasing penalty parameter (Lemma 4.11, p. 14).
Derive the parameter update rule from the perturbation terms of a perturbed-Newton error bound (Theorem 4.25, pp. 25-26).
Plot log residuals over the last ten iterations of all solved runs as empirical rate evidence (p. 31).
Guard infeasibility verdicts with an extra condition (rho_k <= rho-bar) that the fast mechanism makes cheap (p. 29).

quotes.text: This last feature of our algorithm—that of having two separate multiplier estimates—is quite unique for an optimization algorithm.
One finds that many of the curves possess slopes of this type, providing empirical evidence for the convergence results in section 4.
